task_spec.description: CVE-2026-47102's root cause was a self-service endpoint whose ownership check was correct ('only your own account') but whose FIELD-level allowlist was missing, letting a caller mass-assign a privileged user_role field on their own record. CVE-2024-5710 let an authenticated caller manage teams other than their own because the access-control check was missing per-team scoping. Verified directly against admin.go: Handler (lines 83-89) wraps every route in requireBearerToken (lines 96-111), a single constant-time comparison against ONE static admin secret -- there is no identity.Verifier lookup anywhere in this package, no notion of 'this caller's own key' versus 'a different key', and upsertVirtualKeyHandler (lines 131-199) applies every POSTed field (KeyHash, BudgetUSD, AllowedModels, RateLimit incl. PerModel) to whatever virtual key `name` the caller specifies, by design -- a full, intentional replace, per the package's own doc comment describing this as 'a deliberately separate credential space' distinct from client-facing virtual keys.
task_spec.verified_against: gateway/internal/admin/admin.go:83-111 (Handler + requireBearerToken, single static-token check, no per-key ownership concept), :131-199 (upsertVirtualKeyHandler applies every field with no allowlist, by design), package doc comment lines 1-14
task_spec.corpus_note: Both LiteLLM CVEs require a narrowly-scoped/self-service caller whose access is supposed to be limited to 'their own' record or team -- that concept does not exist anywhere in Kelvran's Admin API v1: it is binary (the one static token grants full mutation rights over every virtual key, or no access at all). The specific 'ownership check correct, field allowlist missing' and 'no per-team scoping' bug SHAPES are therefore not currently reproducible against this surface, verified by direct code reading rather than assumed. This is a real, honestly-verified fact about today's code, not evidence of a hidden vulnerability -- but it is also a real regression guard for the future: if Kelvran ever adds a narrower-scoped or self-service key-mutation path (e.g. letting a caller rotate only their own key's metadata), that new path must enforce BOTH an ownership check AND a strict per-field allowlist from day one, per exactly the CVE-2026-47102 pattern -- a bare 'own record only' check would not be sufficient on its own, as that CVE itself demonstrates.

task_spec.description: SkillBloat demonstrates a malicious agent skill inflating a real multi-step coding-agent task's token consumption 26.39x (cost $0.21 -> $5.41) with every individual call unremarkable in isolation -- a stress test for whether a gateway's budget cap is checked before EVERY completion call in a long agentic run, or only once at session start. Verified directly: HandleChatCompletion (dataplane.go line 813) calls p.budget.Allow at line 870, and HandleChatCompletionStream (streaming.go line 61) calls the same p.budget.Allow at streaming.go line 109 -- both are the sole entry points for a completion call, both check unconditionally on every invocation, and neither reads from nor writes to any run-scoped cache of a prior Allow decision (no such cache exists anywhere in dataplane.Pipeline). A multi-step agentic run realized as N separate HTTP requests therefore re-checks Allow N times, never once for the whole run.
task_spec.verified_against: gateway/internal/gateway/dataplane/dataplane.go:813 (HandleChatCompletion), :870 (Allow call site); gateway/internal/gateway/dataplane/streaming.go:61 (HandleChatCompletionStream), :109 (Allow call site)
task_spec.corpus_note: This directly resolves the research's own stated open question favorably: Kelvran's per-request architecture (one HTTP request per completion call, no run/session object spanning several calls) means there is structurally no 'check once at run start' shortcut to exploit in the first place -- every individual completion call within a SkillBloat-style amplified run independently hits the real budget check. This does NOT mean a SkillBloat-style attack is fully mitigated: see the sibling case costabuse-no-cost-velocity-anomaly-signal for the real, honestly-named gap this same finding also surfaces (no anomaly signal below the flat cap), and see costabuse-budget-allow-record-toctou-race for how the per-call check itself is currently racy under concurrent load.

task_spec.description: FIXED. checkRateLimit(ctx, vk, req.Model) (dataplane.go) runs BEFORE routing/fallback resolution, keyed exclusively on req.Model -- the client's originally-requested model, per docs/rfcs/2026-09-07-gateway-multi-dimensional-rate-limits.md's own PerModel design ('checked before falling back to this key's own default bucket'). Revision 1 found no equivalent re-check anywhere after a fallback_chains hop switches to a different actual model. What changed: fallback.go's attemptFallbackChain now takes a new `rateLimitOK func(model string) bool` parameter, called with each candidate target's own Deployment.Model immediately before that target is actually attempted -- after the pre-existing router.IsHealthy check and the consecutiveFailures circuit breaker, mirroring that exact established 'skip without ever attempting, without charging any backoff' pattern. Both real call sites -- dataplane.go's runMissPath (the buffered path) and streaming.go's streamDeploymentWithFallback -- now supply a closure backed by the new Pipeline.checkFallbackTargetRateLimit(ctx, keyID, model) helper, which calls p.limiter.AllowForModel(ctx, keyID, model) (the RPM dimension only; see the new, explicitly-scoped-out sibling case costabuse-tpm-no-permodel-dimension-crossmodel-fallback-gap for why TPM is NOT also covered here). A false result skips that target exactly like a router-unhealthy one: no consecutiveFailures/realAttempts increment, no inter-hop backoff sleep charged, never counted as a real attempt -- so a rate-limited hop never blocks the walk from continuing on to a later, unaffected target in the same configured chain. A rate-limiter backend error fails OPEN (matching checkRateLimit's own pre-existing 'fail-open, not fail-closed' policy for the identical reason), never silently removing a fallback target for an infra reason unrelated to its real rate-limit status.

task_spec.description: budget.Tracker.reservationAmountLocked reserves a key's own historical average real cost once billing history exists (billedCount > 0), or -- on a cold start, billedCount == 0 -- the FULL remaining headroom under the cap. docs/rfcs/2026-09-08-gateway-budget-ratelimit-toctou-fix.md's own 'Alternatives Considered' section explicitly rejected a smaller, proportional cold-start reservation specifically because it 'fails to bound admission to the required "at most one"' for exactly this shape -- meaning the documented, INTENDED design is that a brand-new key's very first concurrent burst admits at most one request until real cost is reconciled. This case verifies that intended behavior's exact real magnitude is as extreme as the RFC's own reasoning implies: the first Reserve call on a cold key consumes 100% of the configured cap as its provisional reservation, not merely 'a large chunk' -- so ANY concurrent sibling call before that first call reconciles is unconditionally rejected, regardless of how small its real eventual cost would be.
task_spec.verified_against: gateway/internal/budget/budget.go:297-302 (reservationAmountLocked: billedCount==0 returns capUSD.Sub(spent[keyID]), the full remaining headroom); budget.go:265-281 (Reserve). A temporary Go probe test in internal/budget, run and deleted before this pass's own final commit: two sequential Reserve calls against the same brand-new key with a $100 cap -- call 1 returns (allowed=true, reserved=true, reservedUSD="100"); call 2, before call 1's Reconcile, returns (allowed=false, reserved=false, reservedUSD="0"); Reconcile(call1) with a real cost of $0.01 leaves SpentUSD="0.01" -- confirming the reservation was exactly the full cap, not a partial/proportional amount, and that it correctly unwinds to the real, tiny cost once reconciled.
task_spec.corpus_note: This is NOT a newly-found bug -- docs/rfcs/2026-09-08-gateway-budget-ratelimit-toctou-fix.md already names and explicitly accepts this exact trade-off by design ('reserve everything, admit one' is the RFC's own phrase), and its Alternatives Considered section already rejected the one candidate fix (proportional reservation) that would have softened it. Encoded here as a PASS case, matching this corpus's established practice of verifying an already-documented, accepted limitation's precise real behavior against the live code (e.g. the guardrail corpus's case 13, adversarial-cache-static-key-decorator-not-applicable) -- not as a FAIL/gap case, since the behavior matches the documented design intent exactly.

task_spec.research_ref: Direct code-reading + live verification exercise against gateway/internal/ratelimit's TokenBucket.ReserveTPM/reservationAmountLocked during this corpus-authoring pass, confirming whether the sibling budget.Tracker.Reserve cold-start-conservatism finding (costabuse-budget-reserve-coldstart-conservatism-verified-exact-magnitude) transfers identically to the TPM dimension -- verified independently rather than assumed to transfer, per this task's own explicit instruction.
task_spec.description: ratelimit.TokenBucket.reservationAmountLocked mirrors budget.Tracker's identical cold-start design: billedCount==0 reserves the bucket's full current balance (b.tokens), not a historical average. An initial assumption that this would behave byte-identically to the budget.Tracker case (a second concurrent call always rejected outright) turned out to be WRONG when first tested against a real, non-frozen clock -- TokenBucket continuously refills based on real elapsed time (refillLocked, called at the top of every ReserveTPM), so even a few microseconds between two sequential Go statements adds back a small amount of balance, letting a second call succeed with a tiny, non-deterministic reservation. Re-verified with a frozen clock (NewTokenBucketWithClock, zero elapsed time) to isolate the TRUE zero-time-elapsed case: under that condition, the behavior is exactly identical to budget.Tracker's -- the second call is flatly rejected. In real production traffic (a real, non-frozen clock, nonzero true elapsed time between concurrent requests), TPM's continuous refill provides a small, real-time-dependent mitigating cushion that budget.Tracker's non-refilling cumulative USD cap structurally cannot have at all -- a genuine, verified DIFFERENCE between the two subsystems' cold-start behavior in practice, not merely a restatement of the same finding twice.
task_spec.verified_against: gateway/internal/ratelimit/ratelimit.go:147-154 (reservationAmountLocked: billedCount==0 returns b.tokens, clamped to zero); ratelimit.go:125-134 (ReserveTPM, calls refillLocked() before checking/reserving). A temporary Go probe test in internal/ratelimit, run and deleted before this pass's own final commit, run twice: once against NewTokenBucket (a real, non-frozen clock) -- call 1 reserved 100000 (the full capacity), call 2 UNEXPECTEDLY succeeded with reservedTokens=1.459792 (a small, real-elapsed-time-dependent refill); once against NewTokenBucketWithClock with a frozen fakeClock (matching this codebase's own existing determinism-testing convention in ratelimit_test.go) -- call 1 reserved 100000, call 2 correctly returned allowed=false, reservedTokens=0, matching budget.Tracker's own behavior exactly under the true zero-elapsed-time condition.

task_spec.research_ref: TPM-specific follow-on investigation, scoped out per this task's own explicit instruction, during the same pass that fixed costabuse-crossmodel-fallback-billed-at-requested-not-served-model-price and costabuse-permodel-ratelimit-bypassed-via-crossmodel-fallback-chain -- same root-cause family (a per-model defense that does not travel with the model actually served across a fallback_chains hop), TPM dimension specifically, per docs/rfcs/2026-09-08-gateway-budget-ratelimit-toctou-fix.md's own note that TPM already carries a Reserve-then-Reconcile bookkeeping obligation RPM does not.
task_spec.description: Investigated for real, not assumed: gateway/internal/ratelimit.KeyConfig declares TPMCapacity/TPMRefillPerSecond as single, key-scoped fields (limiter.go) -- there is no TPM analog of KeyConfig.PerModel at all. KeyLimiter.ReserveTPM/ReconcileTPM (limiter.go) and the TokenBucket.ReserveTPM/ReconcileTPM/reservationAmountLocked they call (ratelimit.go) all take keyID alone, never a model parameter; checkRateLimit's own ReserveTPM call site (dataplane.go) is `p.limiter.ReserveTPM(vk.ID)`, with no model argument to even key a per-model bucket on. This means the RPM fix this same pass shipped (a `rateLimitOK func(model string) bool` closure attemptFallbackChain consults immediately before each real fallback attempt) has structurally nothing to mirror for TPM: there is no PerModel TPM bucket for that closure to check against, because the feature itself does not exist, for ANY access path (direct or via fallback) -- this is a feature absence, not an enforcement-ordering bug in an existing check. Separately, TPM's own RECONCILIATION already correctly uses the response's REAL token count (resp.Usage.TotalTokens, applied via ReconcileTPM regardless of which model served the request) -- since TPM counts raw tokens, not dollars, there is no model-price-table-style mispricing analogous to the cost-accounting sibling gap either. If a PerModel TPM feature were ever added to mirror RPM's, a correct fallback-hop-aware version of it would need materially more than this pass's stateless per-attempt RPM check: TPM's own check is a RESERVATION (a provisional debit that must later be reconciled with real usage), so a fallback-aware PerModel TPM check would need to (a) reserve against a candidate hop's own per-model bucket before attempting it, (b) release that reservation if the walk moves on to yet another target rather than using it, and (c) thread the FINAL, successfully-used hop's own (bucket key, reservedTokens) pair all the way back out through attemptFallbackChain -> runMissPath/streamDeploymentWithFallback -> HandleChatCompletion/HandleChatCompletionStream -> finalize's ReconcileTPM call, replacing the single flat tpmReserved/tpmReservedTokens pair those call sites carry today (reserved once, before routing ever runs) with one that can point at any of N candidate hops' own bucket. That is a genuinely deeper, multi-call-site plumbing change than mirroring an existing atomic, non-reserving check (RPM's Allow) immediately before a real call -- explicitly not attempted in this pass, per this task's own instruction to scope out rather than rush a half-correct fix for a sub-part that needs a materially deeper redesign.
task_spec.verified_against: gateway/internal/ratelimit/limiter.go (KeyConfig struct: TPMCapacity/TPMRefillPerSecond are single fields, PerModel exists only for RPM; ReserveTPM(keyID string)/ReconcileTPM(keyID string, ...), neither takes a model parameter); gateway/internal/ratelimit/ratelimit.go (TokenBucket.ReserveTPM/ReconcileTPM/reservationAmountLocked, all keyed on the bucket alone, no model concept); gateway/internal/gateway/dataplane/dataplane.go's checkRateLimit (`p.limiter.ReserveTPM(vk.ID)` -- no model argument) and finalize's ReconcileTPM call (`p.limiter.ReconcileTPM(vk.ID, tpmReservedTokens, realTokens)`, realTokens = resp.Usage.TotalTokens, applied regardless of which model served the request); docs/rfcs/2026-09-08-gateway-budget-ratelimit-toctou-fix.md (documents TPM's own Reserve-then-Reconcile design, the bookkeeping obligation this case's own reasoning turns on); the sibling, now-fixed costabuse-permodel-ratelimit-bypassed-via-crossmodel-fallback-chain case's own fix (fallback.go's attemptFallbackChain rateLimitOK parameter), read in full to confirm it genuinely has no TPM equivalent to extend.
task_spec.corpus_note: Honestly scoped out, per this task's own explicit instruction: a well-scoped partial fix (the RPM fix and the cost-accounting fix, both shipped this same pass) beats a rushed, half-correct attempt at also retrofitting a PerModel TPM dimension and its fallback-hop-aware re-targeting under time pressure. This case exists so the gap is captured as a new, clearly-named, honestly-scoped FAIL entry rather than silently lost -- matching this project's own established discipline (Cache L3-lite deferring real embeddings, Guardrails deferring NER) of naming a deferred sub-part explicitly rather than letting it vanish. Not a regression: no PerModel TPM feature existed before this pass either, so nothing was broken or narrowed -- this is a pre-existing absence, newly documented. Distinct from the sibling costabuse-ratelimit-tpm-reserve-coldstart-conservatism-verified-exact-magnitude case, which verifies TPM's own reservation-sizing timing behavior in isolation and has nothing to do with cross-model fallback or a PerModel dimension. RESEARCHED 2026-09-09, per docs/upgrade-research/gateway-tpm-permodel-fallback-2026-09-09.md: confirmed this gap is industry-wide and structurally hard, not a Kelvran-specific oversight. No production LLM gateway surveyed (LiteLLM, Kong AI Gateway, Envoy AI Gateway, Bifrost, TensorZero, Helicone) implements reservation-transfer bookkeeping for token-rate limits across a fallback/retry hop -- the field either debits tokens retrospectively (no pre-call reservation at all, e.g. Envoy AI Gateway, Kong's cost strategy, Bifrost) or ships the identical gap shape as a documented, unfixed limitation (Kong: "the request may succeed even if the final model has reached its limit" after a failover). Real exposure is bounded, not open-ended: the now-fixed per-model RPM check (checkFallbackTargetRateLimit) and the pre-existing key-level TPM ceiling (ReserveTPM(vk.ID), reserved once pre-routing) both still apply on every fallback hop today, so an adversary cannot drive unbounded token throughput through a fallback chain even without per-model TPM -- what is missing is only an operator's ability to cap ONE specific model's token throughput independently of the key's aggregate cap, a cost-governance-granularity gap, not an open door to unbounded adversarial cost/DoS. Decision: defer this gap a second time, explicitly, with this research as the justification -- do not build mid-chain TPM reservation-transfer, since it would be a genuinely novel mechanism with zero production precedent to validate its shape against. A real, optional, separately-scoped follow-up remains available if desired: extend PerModel to TPM for the DIRECT (non-fallback) path only, explicitly excluding fallback hops from that check's coverage the same way the RPM fix's own checkFallbackTargetRateLimit is explicitly scoped IN to fallback hops today.

reference: an operator who needs to bound TOKEN THROUGHPUT (not just request rate) specifically for an expensive model reached via a cross-model fallback_chains hop has no per-model TPM cap to configure at all today, on any access path -- and retrofitting one correctly would require re-targeting TPM's own Reserve-then-Reconcile bookkeeping mid-fallback-walk (release the pre-routing reservation, reserve against the actually-served hop's own bucket, and thread the final reservation state back out to finalize's ReconcileTPM call), a materially deeper change than the stateless per-attempt RPM check this same pass added to attemptFallbackChain -- explicitly scoped out of this pass, not fixed
